llm.summary: The skill largely matches its stated purpose (strategy/templates for lead generation) but contains packaging and metadata inconsistencies and includes install/test scripts that warrant manual review before running.

dimensions.detail: Name/description and SKILL.md describe a strategy/automation template product for Russian lead generation and list integrations (amoCRM, Bitrix24, HubSpot, Google Sheets, Telegram, Apollo, Findymail, TargetHunter). The listed optional environment variables (API keys/tokens) are proportionate for those integrations. However the SKILL.md metadata sets network_behavior: makes_requests: false while the product claims 'integration-ready' and lists many external services — this is internally inconsistent and worth clarifying (the skill may only provide instructions/templates rather than make requests itself).
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

dimensions.detail: SKILL.md and docs consistently state the package provides prompts, templates, and guidance and explicitly say it does not automatically send messages or perform remote integrations (hands remain on the user/integration layer). That keeps runtime instruction scope reasonable. Still, many triggers reference parsing/search/outreach commands which could be interpreted by an agent to call external services if the agent is given keys — the instructions are broad enough that a misconfigured agent could attempt network actions.
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: Registry shows 'no install spec' (instruction-only), but the package contains build.sh, install.sh, and test/smoke-test.sh. build.sh expects .env.example and other files when creating a release ZIP, yet .env.example is not present in the manifest — this indicates sloppy packaging (build will fail) or an omitted file. Presence of install.sh and smoke-test.sh means a user could run scripts that modify the system; you should inspect those scripts before executing. The lack of a declared install mechanism plus executable scripts increases the risk if you run them blindly.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: SKILL.md metadata lists many API keys/tokens (ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, OPENAI_API_KEY, TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN, GOOGLE_SHEETS_CREDENTIALS, AMOCRM_ACCESS_TOKEN, BITRIX24_WEBHOOK_URL, APOLLO_API_KEY, FINDYMAIL_API_KEY, TARGETHUNTER_TOKEN). These map to claimed integrations and are reasonable as optional credentials. The registry-level metadata reports 'required env vars: none', which is coherent (they are optional). Still, the package does not document exactly where/when these keys would be used at runtime, and SKILL.md claims no outgoing requests — another inconsistency to clarify before supplying secrets.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: The skill does not request always: true and has no declared required config paths or required binaries. It appears to be a content/instruction package rather than a persistent background agent. That said, shipped install/test scripts could create files or perform actions if executed locally — so avoid running them without review.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

llm.guidance: This skill looks like a content-rich, Russian-market lead-gen toolbox (prompts, templates, config.yaml) rather than an autonomous networked integration — but there are some red flags you should address before installing or running anything: 1) Do not run install.sh, build.sh, or test/smoke-test.sh until you inspect them line-by-line. build.sh references .env.example which is missing from the package; that suggests the package is incomplete or packaged incorrectly. 2) If you plan to supply API keys (Telegram, Google Sheets, CRM tokens, OpenAI/Anthropic), treat them as sensitive: confirm exactly where the keys are used, and only provide them to components you control. 3) Clarify the network behavior with the author: SKILL.md lists integrations but also declares makes_requests: false — ask whether the skill will ever call external APIs autonomously. 4) Run any scripts in an isolated test environment (container or VM) and inspect their content first. 5) If you need higher assurance, ask the maintainer for an updated package that includes .env.example (or remove references to missing files), a clear install spec, and an explicit statement about when network calls occur. If you cannot get that, treat the package as instruction-only (safe to read) but risky to execute.
